episode.throughLine: After a failed business trip and fear of relapse, a man found another person with the same problem, then continued mutual-help work despite setbacks.

facts.statement: Bill Wilson was thirty-nine in May1935; this draft follows that same year to September, within the installed1934–1935 stage.

sourceRefs.locator: Origins: approaching thirty-nine before December 1934; 1935 gatehouse entry.

facts.statement: The founding account places Wilson in a hotel after a business venture failed, with little money and worry about his hotel bill.
The same account describes discouragement, loneliness, attraction to the bar's company, and fear of resuming drinking.

sourceRefs.locator: p. 154, paragraphs beginning Bitterly discouraged and One dismal afternoon.

facts.statement: He turned to a church directory and telephoned a minister; referrals led to Henrietta Seiberling and an arranged meeting.

sourceRefs.locator: Paragraphs beginning A call to a local minister and Henry later orchestrated.
1935,A business trip to Akron: church directory aim, telephone referral.

facts.statement: Wilson and Dr. Bob Smith met at Seiberling's gatehouse on May 12, 1935, exchanging their experiences over several hours.
Smith later drank again; the early partnership did not mean an immediate uninterrupted change for both men.

sourceRefs.locator: pp. 155–156, invitation home and subsequent drinking.

facts.statement: The two men called a hospital and then visited a patient, sharing their own drinking experiences; the patient initially doubted that this could help.

sourceRefs.locator: pp. 156–158, hospital call and first bedside conversation.

facts.statement: The founding account describes failed efforts to reach others and Wilson's eventual return home. AA Archives places his departure in September1935; he continued mutual-help efforts in New York.

sourceRefs.locator: pp. 158–159, several failures and three-month stay.
p.2, By the time Bill left Akron in September paragraph and following1954 chronology excerpt.

facts.statement: Bill Wilson and Robert Smith were co-founders of Alcoholics Anonymous.

sourceRefs.locator: p. 155, explanatory footnote identifying both men.

arc.canonicalText: At thirty-nine, he was in a hotel after a business venture had failed. He had little money and a hotel bill to pay. He was far from home.
arc.sourceNote: Short source-led founding vignette. Wilson's continued shared work, not another patient's conversion, supplies the modest change. No claimed cure, last-drink date, religious requirement or clinical recommendation.

arc.canonicalText: The founding account describes his wish for company and the bar nearby. He considered going in, then became afraid he would drink again. He had been sober only months.
arc.sourceNote: Short source-led founding vignette. Wilson's continued shared work, not another patient's conversion, supplies the modest change. No claimed cure, last-drink date, religious requirement or clinical recommendation.

arc.canonicalText: He turned to a directory of churches and telephoned a minister. The referrals led to a woman who arranged a meeting with another man struggling with alcohol. He had someone to meet.
arc.sourceNote: Short source-led founding vignette. Wilson's continued shared work, not another patient's conversion, supplies the modest change. No claimed cure, last-drink date, religious requirement or clinical recommendation.

arc.canonicalText: They talked for hours about their drinking and what they had experienced. The other man was a doctor, and the meeting did not end his difficulty. He later drank again.
arc.sourceNote: Short source-led founding vignette. Wilson's continued shared work, not another patient's conversion, supplies the modest change. No claimed cure, last-drink date, religious requirement or clinical recommendation.

arc.canonicalText: The two men continued together, calling a hospital and visiting a patient. They talked about their own drinking experiences. The patient was doubtful.
arc.sourceNote: Short source-led founding vignette. Wilson's continued shared work, not another patient's conversion, supplies the modest change. No claimed cure, last-drink date, religious requirement or clinical recommendation.

arc.canonicalText: Their efforts to reach people included failures as well as the beginnings of a group. When he went home later that year, he continued looking for people he might help. There was more work.
arc.sourceNote: Short source-led founding vignette. Wilson's continued shared work, not another patient's conversion, supplies the modest change. No claimed cure, last-drink date, religious requirement or clinical recommendation.

arc.canonicalText:
His name was Bill Wilson.

He co-founded Alcoholics Anonymous with Robert Smith.

Your life is not theirs. But a piece of this story may still sit beside you.

You are allowed to need company.
